pos: n. (the Cistercian system by which each abbey was a daughter of the house that founded it, and answerable to its abbot)
etymology: Latin filius, a son, and filiatio, the relation of a son; the genealogy of houses.
biblical_def: Filiation was the Cistercian constitutional device: every new abbey was founded by a party of monks sent from an existing house, remained the daughter of that house for ever, and was visited annually by its abbot, who was in turn visited by his own mother house, the whole tree running back to Cîteaux. Five lines — La Ferté, Pontigny, Clairvaux, Morimond and Cîteaux itself — organised some seven hundred abbeys across Europe without a central bureaucracy. It is an elegant answer to a real problem, and its instincts are scriptural: that oversight should be personal and genealogical rather than remote, and that no leader should be unvisited. “Let us go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do” (Act 15:36) is filiation in embryo. The limitation is that lineage is not grace. A daughter house inherited a constitution, not a conversion, and the Cistercian decline came precisely through houses that kept their filiation perfectly and lost their religion entirely. “Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (Joh 1:13) is the distinction every institutional family forgets.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines filiation as the relation of a son to a father, correlative to paternity; filial as pertaining to a son or daughter, becoming a child in relation to his parents; and lineage as race, progeny, descendants in a line from a common progenitor.
webster_full: FILIATION, n. The relation of a son to a father; correlative to paternity.
FILIAL, a. Pertaining to a son or daughter; becoming a child in relation to his parents; as filial duty or obedience.
LINEAGE, n. Race; progeny; descendants in a line from a common progenitor.
DESCENT, n. Lineage; the line of generation, reckoned downward; also, a proceeding from an original or progenitor.
MOTHER, n. A female parent; especially, one of the human race; also, the female superior of a religious house.
scriptures: And some days after Paul said unto Barnabas, Let us go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do.
Joh 1:13
Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
Joh 3:6
That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.
Mat 3:9
And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.
corruption_summary: The Cistercian genealogy of mother and daughter houses: personal oversight without a bureaucracy, and a lineage that could be kept perfectly while the religion was lost.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the confidence of descent. John the Baptist met it in its original form and would not allow it: “And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham” (Mat 3:9). An abbey that could trace itself to Clairvaux had a pedigree and not a promise, and “That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit” (Joh 3:6) holds for institutions as for men.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one filiation got right: oversight by someone who comes in person, knows the house, and is himself visited. Denominations that have replaced that with a form returned annually to an office have the accountability of paper and should admit it.
roots_summary: Latin filius, a son; Greek huios (G5207), a son; Greek teknon (G5043), a child; Greek genea (G1074), a generation; Hebrew ben (H1121), a son.
roots_lines: Latin filiatio — sonship, the relation of son to father; the name of the whole Cistercian structure.
Greek huios (G5207) — a son, with the note of standing and heirship.
Greek teknon (G5043) — a child, with the note of birth; “born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh” (Joh 1:13).
Hebrew ben (H1121) — a son; the Hebrew genealogies run on this word.
Greek anagennao (G313) — to beget again; the new birth, which no lineage confers.
usage: “and see how they do” (Act 15:36) — the personal visitation filiation institutionalised.
“We have Abraham to our father” (Mat 3:9) — the false confidence of descent.
“that which is born of the Spirit is spirit” (Joh 3:6) — the birth an institution cannot transmit.

pos: n. (the privilege freeing an abbey or order from the jurisdiction of the local bishop, answerable only to the pope)
etymology: Latin exemptio, a taking out, from eximere, to take out; the house taken out of the bishop's jurisdiction.
biblical_def: Exemption was the privilege by which an abbey, or a whole order, was taken out of its bishop's jurisdiction and made answerable directly to Rome. Cluny obtained it, the Cistercians held it, the friars lived by it, and it was among the most contested privileges in medieval church law, because a bishop could not correct what he could not visit and Rome was far away. The result was predictable and is instructive about church polity generally. Scripture places oversight locally and makes it answerable: elders are appointed “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5), and they watch over a flock they know — “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers” (Act 20:28). A body answerable only to a distant authority is in practice answerable to none, and “Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he” (Pro 29:18) describes the result. Exemption did protect genuine reform from hostile local prelates, which is the honest case for it; but a privilege that removes correction will in the end be used by those who most need it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exemption as the act of exempting, the state of being free from a charge or duty to which others are subject; exempt as free, clear, not liable to; and jurisdiction as the legal power of judging and determining.
webster_full: EXEMPTION, n. The act of exempting; the state of being exempt; freedom from any service, charge, burden, tax, evil or requisition, to which others are subject.
EXEMPT, a. Free; clear; not liable to; not subject; as, no man is exempt from the laws of nature.
JURISDICTION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing the laws and distributing justice.
PRIVILEGE, n. A particular and peculiar benefit or advantage enjoyed by a person, company or society, beyond the common advantages of other citizens.
CORRECT, v.t. To make right; to rectify; to bring to the standard of truth; also, to punish for faults or deviations.
scriptures: Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he.

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
corruption_summary: Freedom from the local bishop, answerable only to a distant Rome: a shield for genuine reform, and in the end a licence for whoever most needed correcting.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is accountability moved out of reach. Scripture's overseers are men who live among those they oversee and who may be approached, examined and if necessary charged; an exempt house answered to an authority a thousand miles off that would never arrive. “Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account” (Heb 13:17) describes a watching that requires proximity and a reckoning that requires a reckoner.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is local, visible, answerable oversight — “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5). Independent congregations and large networks alike can manufacture their own exemption, the one by recognising no outside correction and the other by placing it too far away to operate.
roots_summary: Latin eximere, to take out; Greek episkopos (G1985), an overseer; Greek presbuteros (G4245), an elder; Greek exousia (G1849), authority; Greek logos (G3056) in the sense of an account.
roots_lines: Latin exemptio — a taking out; the house removed from its bishop's reach.
Greek episkopos (G1985) — an overseer; “the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers” (Act 20:28).
Greek presbuteros (G4245) — an elder; “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5).
Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, the right to act; what exemption transferred.
Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to submit; the duty exemption suspended.
usage: “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) — oversight located where the people are.
“as they that must give account” (Heb 13:17) — a reckoning that needs someone present to receive it.
“he that keepeth the law, happy is he” (Pro 29:18) — the blessing of being under a rule one cannot evade.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Berry, central France, founded 1136 as a daughter of Clairvaux)
etymology: French noir, black, and lac, a lake: the black lake, from the marshy ground beside the Cher that the monks drained.
biblical_def: Noirlac was founded in 1136 beside the river Cher in Berry, a daughter of Clairvaux settled under Bernard's own direction, and it survives as one of the most complete Cistercian complexes in France — church, cloister, chapter house, refectory and dormitory all standing. Its later history is the one worth telling. Suppressed at the Revolution, the abbey was sold and spent the nineteenth century as a porcelain factory, with kilns in the nave and workers' families housed in the monks' range, before the state bought it back in 1909. A building raised for the praise of God spent a hundred years making china. It is hard to read that without hearing “There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down” (Mat 24:2), spoken of a far greater sanctuary; and “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1) is the standing comment on every consecrated stone. Noirlac's stones outlasted its religion by a century and a half, which is a warning rather than a triumph.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines abbey as a monastery or society of persons of either sex, secluded from the world and devoted to religion; and lake as a large and extensive collection of water contained in a cavity or hollow of the earth.
webster_full: ABBEY, n. A monastery or society of persons of either sex, secluded from the world and devoted to religion. The males are called monks, and governed by an abbot; the females are called nuns, and governed by an abbess.
LAKE, n. A large and extensive collection of water contained in a cavity or hollow of the earth.
MARSH, n. A tract of soft wet land, or a tract of land occasionally overflowed by water, or covered with water.
FACTORY, n. A house or place where factors reside; also, a building appropriated to the manufacture of goods.
SUPPRESS, v.t. To crush; to subdue; to destroy; to put an end to.
scriptures: Mat 24:2
And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down.
A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
Hag 1:4
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
And this word, Yet once more, signifieth the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that are made, that those things which cannot be shaken may remain.
corruption_summary: A Clairvaux daughter of 1136 whose buildings survive almost whole: suppressed at the Revolution and run as a porcelain factory for a century, its stones outlasting its religion.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that buildings are not the church and cannot be made to be. “the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that are made, that those things which cannot be shaken may remain” (Heb 12:27) sorts the two categories, and a nave full of kilns is a blunt illustration of which side masonry falls on.

The live warning is complacency about endowment. Noirlac was wealthy, well built and perfectly regular, and none of that preserved a living faith in it. “except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psa 127:1) applies to institutions that have everything except the thing they were founded for — and most of them do not notice until the kilns arrive.
roots_summary: French noir lac, black lake; Hebrew bayith (H1004), a house; Hebrew eben (H68), a stone; Greek oikos (G3624), a house; Greek lithos (G3037), a stone.
roots_lines: French noir lac — the black lake; the marsh the monks drained to build.
Hebrew bayith (H1004) — a house, and so a household and a dynasty; “Except the LORD build the house” (Psa 127:1).
Hebrew eben (H68) — a stone; the material of altars, memorials and temples alike.
Greek lithos (G3037) — a stone; “There shall not be left here one stone upon another” (Mat 24:2).
Greek oikodomeo (G3618) — to build; used in the New Testament far more of people than of buildings.
usage: “they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1) — the verdict on a house raised without God.
“that shall not be thrown down” (Mat 24:2) — said of the temple, and true of every abbey.
“those things which cannot be shaken may remain” (Heb 12:27) — the sorting that outlasts masonry.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey on the Durance in Provence, founded 1144; one of the three Cistercian sisters of Provence)
etymology: Latin silva cannarum, the forest of reeds, from the reed beds of the Durance marshes where it was built.
biblical_def: Silvacane was founded in 1144 on the north bank of the Durance in Provence, a daughter of Morimond, and takes its name from the reed forest of the marsh its monks drained. With Sénanque and Le Thoronet it is one of the three Cistercian houses of Provence whose austere buildings survive, and its church is the plainest of the three: no tower, no sculpture, no coloured glass, light handled as the only ornament. The site is the point. A Cistercian foundation charter typically specified waste ground, and the order's preference for marsh, scrub and fen was both an ascetic choice and an agricultural one, since drained marsh is excellent land. Scripture has a good deal to say about such transformations, and says it of God rather than of monks: “And the parched ground shall become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water: in the habitation of dragons, where each lay, shall be grass with reeds and rushes” (Isa 35:7). The reed itself is Scripture's image of the frail thing God will not break: “A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench” (Isa 42:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reed as the common name of many aquatic plants, most of them large grasses; marsh as a tract of soft wet land; and austere as severe, harsh, rigid, applied to manners and discipline.
webster_full: REED, n. The common name of many aquatic plants; most of them large grasses, with hollow jointed stems.
MARSH, n. A tract of soft wet land, or a tract of land occasionally overflowed by water, or covered with water.
AUSTERE, a. Severe; harsh; rigid; stern; applied to persons, and to their manners and discipline.
DRAIN, v.t. To filter; to cause to pass through some porous substance; also, to make dry, as land, by cutting channels.
SILVAN, a. Pertaining to a wood or grove; woody; abounding with woods.
scriptures: Isa 35:7
And the parched ground shall become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water: in the habitation of dragons, where each lay, shall be grass with reeds and rushes.
Isa 42:3
A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth.
A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory.
And the LORD shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones: and thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not.
corruption_summary: A Provencal Cistercian house of 1144 built on a reed marsh: plain stone and light for ornament, named for the frail plant Scripture says God will not break.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the gentleness of God toward what is nearly broken. “A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory” (Mat 12:20) is Matthew's portrait of Christ, and it is a better word to take from a reed marsh than any lesson in austerity.

The live caution is the pride that plainness breeds. A church stripped of ornament can become as self-congratulatory as a gilded one, and the Cistercian polemic against Cluniac decoration occasionally reads that way. “thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not” (Isa 58:11) promises fruitfulness to the obedient, not to the austere.
roots_summary: Latin silva cannarum, forest of reeds; Hebrew qaneh (H7070), a reed; Hebrew agam (H98), a pool or marsh; Greek kalamos (G2563), a reed; Hebrew gome (H1573), a bulrush.
roots_lines: Latin silva cannarum — forest of reeds; the marsh the house is named for.
Hebrew qaneh (H7070) — a reed, a stalk, a measuring cane; “A bruised reed shall he not break” (Isa 42:3).
Greek kalamos (G2563) — a reed; “and smoking flax shall he not quench” (Mat 12:20).
Hebrew agam (H98) — a pool, a marsh; “the parched ground shall become a pool” (Isa 35:7).
Hebrew gome (H1573) — a bulrush; the plant of Moses' ark and of Isaiah's bowed head.
usage: “shall be grass with reeds and rushes” (Isa 35:7) — the marsh transformed, in God's hand rather than a monk's.
“the smoking flax shall he not quench” (Isa 42:3) — the mercy the reed stands for.
“like a watered garden” (Isa 58:11) — the fruitfulness promised to obedience.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in a fold of the Vaucluse hills in Provence, founded 1148 and still a monastic community)
etymology: From Provençal, probably from a root meaning a dry or sandy valley; the abbey takes its name from the narrow combe it fills.
biblical_def: Sénanque was founded in 1148 in a steep dry combe of the Vaucluse, a daughter of Mazan, and is the only one of the three Provencal sisters still occupied by a monastic community, having been reoccupied in the twentieth century. It is the most photographed abbey in France because of the lavender field in front of it, and that accident of popularity is worth a word, since the flowers in the photograph last six weeks and the building has lasted nine hundred years — while Scripture insists that neither is the enduring thing. “All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field” (Isa 40:6) and “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) set the proportion exactly. Christ draws the other lesson from the same kind of field: “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin” (Mat 6:28) and “That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these” (Mat 6:29). A Cistercian house in a flowering valley was a good place to learn both, and it is not clear that its visitors do.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines flower as the delicate and gaily colored leaves or petals of a plant, and figuratively the prime or best part; valley as a hollow or low tract of land between hills; and fade as to lose color, to wither, to decay.
webster_full: FLOWER, n. In botany, that part of a plant which contains the organs of generation; also, the delicate and gaily colored leaves or petals; figuratively, the prime, the choicest part.
VALLEY, n. A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.
FADE, v.i. To lose color; to lose freshness; to wither, as a plant; to decline; to perish gradually.
LILY, n. A genus of plants of many species, bearing beautiful flowers.
WITHER, v.i. To fade; to lose its native freshness; to become sapless; to dry.
scriptures: Isa 40:6
The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field:
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
Mat 6:28
And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:
Mat 6:29
And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
corruption_summary: A Provencal house of 1148 in a dry combe, still occupied: the most photographed abbey in France, and a good place to learn that neither flower nor masonry endures.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Isaiah states in the same breath as the flower. “but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) is the only durable thing named in the passage, and a tourist industry built on a six-week bloom in front of a nine-century wall illustrates the point rather than teaching it.

The live misuse is aesthetic Christianity: the abbey as atmosphere, the lavender as mood, monasticism admired as a style by people who would reject every proposition it was built on. Christ's own use of a flowering field is moral and not decorative — “And why take ye thought for raiment?” (Mat 6:28) — and he draws from it a command about anxiety, not a photograph.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsits (H6731), a flower; Hebrew chatsir (H2682), grass; Greek anthos (G438), a flower; Greek krinon (G2918), a lily; Hebrew dabar (H1697), a word.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsits (H6731) — a blossom or flower; “as the flower of the field” (Isa 40:6).
Hebrew chatsir (H2682) — grass, herbage; “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth” (Isa 40:8).
Greek krinon (G2918) — a lily; “Consider the lilies of the field” (Mat 6:28).
Greek anthos (G438) — a flower; Peter quotes Isaiah with this word of all human glory.
Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, a matter; the one thing in the passage that stands.
usage: “All flesh is grass” (Isa 40:6) — the measure of every beautiful thing, abbeys included.
“even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these” (Mat 6:29) — the field above the palace.
“the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) — the only durable item on the list.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the wooded hills of Provence, founded in the 1130s and built about 1160-1190)
etymology: From Provençal, probably a diminutive related to a hill or height; the abbey is named from its locality, Le Thoronet.
biblical_def: Le Thoronet is the oldest of the three Cistercian sisters of Provence, settled in the 1130s and built between about 1160 and 1190 in bare local limestone. It is the most severe building of the three and the most famous among architects: its unadorned volumes and extraordinary acoustic — a long reverberation that forces the choir to sing slowly and together — were studied by Le Corbusier, and the abbey has become a standard text in the argument that restraint can be more eloquent than ornament. A Protestant can agree with the aesthetic judgment and still ask the prior question, which is what the building is for. Stone cannot praise and cannot hear. “The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork” (Psa 19:1) gives creation a voice of its own; and Christ's remark about the stones is a rebuke to men, not a promise to masonry: “I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out” (Luk 19:40). The acoustic is a servant of the singers, and a church is “built up a spiritual house” (1Pe 2:5) out of people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines acoustic as pertaining to the ears, to the sense of hearing, or to the doctrine of sounds; echo as a sound reflected or reverberated from a solid body; and stone as a concretion of earthy or mineral matter.
webster_full: ACOUSTIC, a. Pertaining to the ears, to the sense of hearing, or to the doctrine of sounds.
ECHO, n. A sound reflected or reverberated from a solid body; sound returned; repercussion of sound.
REVERBERATE, v.t. To return, as sound; to send back; to echo.
STONE, n. A concretion of earthy or mineral matter; also, a small mass of such matter.
SIMPLICITY, n. Singleness; the state of being unmixed or uncompounded; plainness; artlessness; freedom from ornament.
scriptures: Psa 19:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
And he answered and said unto them, I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out.
Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.
Hab 2:20
But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him.
corruption_summary: The severest of the Provencal Cistercian houses, famous for its acoustic: eloquent restraint in stone, which still cannot praise and cannot hear.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is reverence of the kind a long reverberation enforces: “But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20). An acoustic that punishes haste is doing a congregation a service, and most modern rooms are built to do the opposite.

The live misuse is the architectural one — Le Thoronet admired as pure form by people indifferent to the psalms it was shaped to carry. The building is a servant and the singers are the church: “Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood” (1Pe 2:5) puts the living stones in the walls and the quarried ones underfoot.
roots_summary: Hebrew eben (H68), a stone; Hebrew damam (H1826), to be silent; Greek lithos (G3037), a stone; Greek siopao (G4623), to keep silence; Hebrew heykal (H1964), a temple.
roots_lines: Hebrew eben (H68) — a stone; the material, and in Scripture also a memorial and a cornerstone.
Hebrew damam (H1826) — to be still, to be silent; “let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20).
Greek lithos (G3037) — a stone; “the stones would immediately cry out” (Luk 19:40).
Greek lithos zon — a living stone; “as lively stones” (1Pe 2:5) is Peter's phrase for Christians.
Hebrew heykal (H1964) — a palace or temple; the house a congregation now is.
usage: “But the LORD is in his holy temple” (Hab 2:20) — the reverence the building was shaped for.
“the firmament sheweth his handywork” (Psa 19:1) — creation's own eloquence, above any architecture.
“built up a spiritual house” (1Pe 2:5) — the only masonry that matters.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Gascony, founded 1151 as a daughter of L'Escaladieu)
etymology: From the Gascon locality on the Baise; the abbey is named for its site in the valley of that river.
biblical_def: Flaran was founded in 1151 beside the Baïse in Gascony, a daughter of L'Escaladieu in the filiation of Morimond, and it is one of the best-preserved Cistercian houses of south-west France — church, cloister and ranges substantially intact. Sold at the Revolution, damaged by fire in 1970 and bought by the department, it now serves as a cultural centre with galleries in the monks' ranges. That is the characteristic fate of a French abbey, and it raises a question a Protestant should answer carefully rather than cheaply. A building put to secular use is not thereby desecrated, because the holiness was never in the stone: Christ's word to the woman of Samaria settles the geography of worship for good, “the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father” (Joh 4:21), and “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:24). Yet nothing in that frees us from grief at an empty church. “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name” (Psa 74:7) is a lament Scripture permits.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sanctuary as a sacred place, particularly among the Israelites the most retired part of the temple; preserve as to keep or save from injury or destruction; and cloister as a place of religious retirement.
webster_full: SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple, where the ark was kept, and where no person entered except the high priest.
PRESERVE, v.t. To keep or save from injury or destruction; to defend from evil; to uphold.
CLOISTER, n. A monastery or nunnery; a house inhabited by monks or nuns; also, a peristyle; an arcade.
SECULAR, a. Pertaining to this present world, or to things not spiritual or holy; worldly; temporal.
DESECRATE, v.t. To divert from a sacred purpose or appropriation; to divest of a sacred character or office.
scriptures: Joh 4:21
Jesus saith unto her, Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father.
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
Psa 74:7
They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground.
God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands;
corruption_summary: A Gascon Cistercian house of 1151, now a cultural centre: the holiness was never in the stone, which leaves the lament over an empty church intact.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Paul preached at Athens: “God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands” (Act 17:24). A Protestant who is scandalised by galleries in a cloister has not yet taken that in; one who feels nothing at all has not taken in Psalm 74.

The live error, on both sides, is to locate the sacred in the fabric. Rome did it by consecration and we do it by sentiment. “they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:24) is the one sentence that dissolves the argument, and it was spoken to a woman asking which mountain was the right one.
roots_summary: Hebrew miqdash (H4720), a sanctuary; Greek naos (G3485), a temple; Greek cheiropoietos (G5499), made with hands; Greek pneuma (G4151), spirit; Hebrew maon (H4583), a dwelling.
roots_lines: Hebrew miqdash (H4720) — a sanctuary, a holy place; “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary” (Psa 74:7).
Greek cheiropoietos (G5499) — made with hands; “dwelleth not in temples made with hands” (Act 17:24).
Greek naos (G3485) — the inner sanctuary; applied by Paul to the believer's body.
Greek pneuma (G4151) — spirit; “God is a Spirit” (Joh 4:24).
Hebrew maon (H4583) — a dwelling, habitation; used of God's own abode, which is not a building.
usage: “ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father” (Joh 4:21) — the end of sacred geography.
“dwelleth not in temples made with hands” (Act 17:24) — Paul at Athens, on buildings.
“they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name” (Psa 74:7) — the lament Scripture allows.

pos: n. (a great abbey in Languedoc, founded 1139 and Cistercian from 1159; after the Revolution its church was used as a wine cellar)
etymology: Latin vallis magna, the great valley; the abbey is named for the broad valley near the Thau lagoon in which it stands.
biblical_def: Valmagne was founded in 1139 near the Étang de Thau in Languedoc, joined the Cistercians in 1159, and grew into one of the wealthiest houses in the south of France, with a soaring Gothic church quite unlike the order's early austerity. Its modern state is the most arresting in this group: after the Revolution the estate passed into private hands as a vineyard, and enormous oak casks were installed in the aisles of the abbey church, where they still stand. Wine is made and sold there. One can hardly ask for a plainer parable, and Scripture supplies the vocabulary for reading it both ways. The vine is Christ's own figure of himself and his people — “I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman” (Joh 15:1) — so a vineyard is no insult to a church. But Isaiah's vineyard song is a judgment: God planted the choicest vine and “he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes” (Isa 5:2). A church that became a cellar is a fair emblem of a house that kept the apparatus of fruitfulness and produced something else.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vineyard as a plantation of vines producing grapes; cellar as a room under a building used as a repository of liquors and provisions; and cask as a close vessel for containing liquors, formed by staves, heading and hoops.
webster_full: VINEYARD, n. A plantation of vines producing grapes; a close or inclosure planted with vines.
CELLAR, n. A room under a building, used as a repository of liquors, provisions and other stores.
CASK, n. A close vessel for containing liquors, formed by staves, heading and hoops.
VINE, n. A plant of the genus Vitis, which produces grapes; also, any climbing plant.
HUSBANDMAN, n. A farmer; a cultivator or tiller of the ground; one who labors in tillage.
scriptures: Joh 15:1
I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.
Isa 5:1
Now will I sing to my wellbeloved a song of my beloved touching his vineyard. My wellbeloved hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill:
Isa 5:2

And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes.
Mat 9:17
Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved.
corruption_summary: A wealthy Languedoc abbey of 1139 whose church now holds wine casks in its aisles: a vineyard is no insult to a church, and Isaiah's vineyard song is a judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is not the casks but the wealth that preceded them. A Cistercian house with a soaring Gothic church had already abandoned the order's founding plainness long before the Revolution arrived, and Isaiah's question stands over it: “My wellbeloved hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill” (Isa 5:1) — every advantage given, and “it brought forth wild grapes” (Isa 5:2).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Christ's own warning about containers. “Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out” (Mat 9:17) is about forms that cannot hold what is poured into them, and a reform movement that had become a great landowner in two centuries is an old bottle by any reckoning.
roots_summary: Latin vallis magna, great valley; Hebrew kerem (H3754), a vineyard; Hebrew gephen (H1612), a vine; Greek ampelos (G288), a vine; Greek georgos (G1092), a husbandman.
roots_lines: Latin vallis magna — the great valley; the house named for its broad site.
Hebrew kerem (H3754) — a vineyard; “a song of my beloved touching his vineyard” (Isa 5:1).
Hebrew gephen (H1612) — a vine; Israel's standing emblem in the prophets.
Greek ampelos (G288) — a vine; “I am the true vine” (Joh 15:1).
Greek georgos (G1092) — a tiller of the soil; “and my Father is the husbandman” (Joh 15:1).
usage: “I am the true vine” (Joh 15:1) — the figure that makes a vineyard no dishonour to a church.
“and it brought forth wild grapes” (Isa 5:2) — the judgment on every advantaged vineyard.
“but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved” (Mat 9:17) — the form that can hold the thing.

pos: n. (an abbey in the Corbieres of Languedoc, founded 1093 and Cistercian from 1145; closely involved in the Albigensian Crusade)
etymology: Old French font froide, the cold spring, from the source in the dry hills on which the abbey was founded.
biblical_def: Fontfroide was founded in 1093 in the arid Corbières hills and affiliated to the Cistercians in 1145, taking its name from a cold spring in a waterless country. It became one of the richest houses in the Midi, and its history is inseparable from the crusade against the Cathars. Two of its monks were papal legates charged with preaching against the heresy; one of them, Pierre de Castelnau, was murdered in 1208, and his death was the occasion for Innocent III to launch the Albigensian Crusade. Another Fontfroide abbot, Arnaud Amalric, led it. The dictionary must say plainly what follows. Heresy is real, and Scripture does not ask the church to be indifferent to it. But the weapon appointed against error is the word, and Christ forbade the other kind by name: “Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52). When the disciples proposed fire on a village that rejected him, “he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” (Luk 9:55), and “For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them” (Luk 9:56).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fountain as a spring, or source of water, the head of a stream; crusade as a military expedition undertaken by Christians for the recovery of the Holy Land; and heresy as a fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine.
webster_full: FOUNTAIN, n. A spring, or source of water; properly, a spring or issuing of water from the earth; the head or source of a stream.
CRUSADE, n. A military expedition undertaken by Christians for the recovery of the Holy Land from the infidels; any romantic undertaking.
HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
LEGATE, n. An ambassador; a cardinal or bishop sent as the pope's representative or commissioner.
PERSECUTE, v.t. To pursue in a manner to injure, vex or afflict; to harass with unjust punishment or penalties for supposed offenses.
scriptures: Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Luk 9:55
But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of.
Luk 9:56
For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them. And they went to another village.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
corruption_summary: A rich Languedoc abbey of 1093 whose legate's murder launched the Albigensian Crusade and whose abbot led it: heresy is real, and the sword was never the weapon against it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the sword in the church's hand, and there is no softening it. Paul names the arsenal and excludes this item: “For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4). A monastery that supplied a crusade with its commander had departed from its own founder, its own rule and its Lord, and the fact that the Cathars held genuinely ruinous doctrine does not alter the judgment by a hair.

The honest second word is that this dictionary does not share the Cathars' faith and will not pretend to. They denied the goodness of creation and the true humanity of Christ, which Scripture settles — “For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:4). One may hold a man's doctrine damnable and his killing murder, and here both are true. The principle to recover is that the only sword the church carries is the Spirit's.
roots_summary: Old French font froide, cold spring; Hebrew mayan (H4599), a spring; Greek machaira (G3162), a sword; Greek sarkikos (G4559), carnal; Greek hairesis (G139), a heresy or faction.
roots_lines: Old French font froide — the cold spring; a waterless country's one asset.
Hebrew mayan (H4599) — a spring, fountain; “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters” (Jer 2:13).
Greek machaira (G3162) — a sword; “Put up again thy sword into his place” (Mat 26:52).
Greek sarkikos (G4559) — fleshly, carnal; “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” (2Co 10:4).
Greek hairesis (G139) — a chosen opinion, a faction; the thing the crusade was aimed at, by the wrong means.
usage: “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52) — Christ disarming his own disciple.
“Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” (Luk 9:55) — said to men proposing fire on a village.
“mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4) — the weapons actually issued.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Languedoc, founded 1114 and Cistercian from 1145; once among the wealthiest in the Midi, now almost wholly destroyed)
etymology: Latin grandis silva, the great wood, through Old French; the abbey is named for the forest it was planted in near Bouillac.
biblical_def: Grandselve was founded in 1114 as a hermitage in the great wood north of Toulouse, became Cistercian in 1145, and grew into one of the richest abbeys of southern France, with granges across Languedoc and a college at Toulouse. Almost nothing of it is left. Sold as building material after the Revolution, it was quarried away, and a fragment of wall and a gate stand where a church longer than many cathedrals once did. The contrast between its wealth and its erasure is the entry's subject, and Scripture has stated the principle too often to need elaborating. “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal” (Mat 6:19), and the alternative in the next verse, “But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt” (Mat 6:20). “He that trusteth in his riches shall fall: but the righteous shall flourish as a branch” (Pro 11:28) sets a tree against a treasury, which is pointed in a house named for a forest.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines forest as an extensive wood, or a large tract of land covered with trees; riches as wealth, opulence, affluence, abundance of lands, goods or money; and ruin as destruction, fall, overthrow, and the remains of a decayed structure.
webster_full: FOREST, n. An extensive wood, or a large tract of land covered with trees.
RICHES, n. Wealth; opulence; affluence; abundance of lands, goods, money or other property.
RUIN, n. Destruction; fall; overthrow; defeat; also, the remains of a decayed or demolished city, house or other work of men.
QUARRY, n. A place, cavern or pit where stones are dug from the earth, or separated from a large mass of rocks.
FLOURISH, v.i. To thrive; to grow luxuriantly; to increase and enlarge, as a healthy growing plant.
scriptures: Mat 6:19
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
Mat 6:20
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
He that trusteth in his riches shall fall: but the righteous shall flourish as a branch.
Jam 4:14
Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
corruption_summary: A Languedoc abbey of 1114 once among the richest in the Midi, quarried away after the Revolution: granges across a province, and a gate left standing.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the accumulation, not the loss. A house founded as a hermitage in a wood and holding granges across a province in two centuries has undergone a change its founders did not intend, and the Cistercian pattern of poverty-then-prosperity-then-decay repeats too often to be accidental. Discipline produces surplus; surplus corrodes discipline. “He that trusteth in his riches shall fall” (Pro 11:28) is the mechanism in six words.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the brevity of every institution. “For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away” (Jam 4:14) is said of a man, and a quarried abbey shows it is no less true of a corporation that held land for six hundred years.
roots_summary: Latin grandis silva, great wood; Hebrew yaar (H3293), a forest; Hebrew osher (H6239), riches; Greek thesauros (G2344), a treasure; Greek atmis (G822), a vapour.
roots_lines: Latin grandis silva — the great wood; the forest that named the house and outlasted it.
Hebrew yaar (H3293) — a forest, wood; “The trees of the LORD are full of sap; the cedars of Lebanon, which he hath planted” (Psa 104:16).
Hebrew osher (H6239) — riches, wealth; “He that trusteth in his riches shall fall” (Pro 11:28).
Greek thesauros (G2344) — a treasure, a storehouse; “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Mat 6:20).
Greek atmis (G822) — a vapour, mist; “It is even a vapour” (Jam 4:14).
usage: “where thieves break through and steal” (Mat 6:19) — the fate of a quarried abbey, stated in advance.
“but the righteous shall flourish as a branch” (Pro 11:28) — a tree set against a treasury.
“and then vanisheth away” (Jam 4:14) — true of men and of six-century corporations.
